ig_carousel_topic.topic: Why your win rate matters less than your ROI
ig_carousel_topic.slide1_text:
You can win 56% of your bets and still lose money.
Here is why win rate alone tells you almost nothing.
ig_carousel_topic.slide2_text:
Most bettors fixate on win rate.
Hit 55% and you think you are beating the book.
But the line you bet and the size of your edge determine whether that 55% is profitable or a slow bleed.
ig_carousel_topic.slide3_text:
ROI captures what win rate ignores: the price you paid.
Betting 55% winners at -140 across the board returns roughly -2% ROI. Betting 53% winners at +110 returns roughly +4% ROI.
The second bettor wins less often and makes more money.
ig_carousel_topic.slide4_text:
Real example from our YTD numbers:
243-204, 54.4% win rate, +37.7u, 9.3% ROI across 41 days.
If we had bet the same record at -120 average juice instead of near-median lines, that 9.3% ROI shrinks to roughly 2%. Same wins. Very different result.
ig_carousel_topic.slide5_text:
Track your average odds alongside your win rate.
If your average winning bet is paying less than your average losing bet costs, a 55% record still works against you.
ROI is the number that settles the argument.
ig_carousel_topic.caption: Win rate is not the scoreboard. ROI is. Our 54.4% record this year means nothing without the +9.3% ROI sitting behind it. This is the number to track.
